summary: This RFC covers the implementation of domain name servers and resolvers, specifies the format of their messages, and discusses how domain names fit existing mail systems and network software. It is an early version of the DNS specification, replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

plainLanguage.summary: Domain names let a program ask for information about a name, such as the address of a host, without knowing where that information is kept. The request goes to a local resolver, which asks name servers on the network until it finds an answer. This RFC describes the pieces and the messages between them.

subtitle: The original specification of the domain name system: how resolvers, name servers and the messages between them work.

tldr.problem: Programs need to turn names such as a host's domain name into the information associated with them, and no agreed message format or procedure existed for doing so across the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a distributed database of names, the resolvers and name servers that read it, the message format they exchange, the maintenance of the authoritative copies, and how the system supports mail.
tldr.outcome: The design became the DNS. The document is from 1983 and warns that its format specifications are preliminary and for explanation only. It was replaced by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The goal of domain names is to provide a mechanism for naming resources so that the names are usable in different hosts, networks, protocol families, internets and administrative organizations. From the user's point of view, domain names are arguments to a local agent, called a resolver, which retrieves information associated with the name; to request a particular kind of information, an appropriate query type is passed to the resolver along with the name. To the user, the domain tree is a single information space.

From the resolver's point of view, the database that makes up the domain space is distributed among various name servers. Different parts of the domain space are stored in different name servers, although a particular data item will usually be stored redundantly in two or more of them. The resolver starts with knowledge of at least one name server; when it processes a user query it asks a known name server for the information, and in return receives either the information or a referral to another name server. Using these referrals the resolver learns the identities and contents of other name servers. Resolvers are responsible for dealing with the distribution of the domain space and with the effects of name server failure by consulting redundant databases elsewhere.

Name servers manage two kinds of data. The first is held in sets called zones, each the complete database for a particular subtree of the domain space; this data is authoritative, and a name server periodically checks that its zones are up to date, obtaining a new copy from master files stored locally or in another name server. The second is cached data acquired by a local resolver, which may be incomplete but improves performance when non-local data is repeatedly accessed, and which is eventually discarded by a timeout. This functional structure isolates the problems of user interface, failure recovery and distribution in the resolvers, and isolates the database update and refresh problems in the name servers.

The memo carries a warning: the format specifications it contains are preliminary and are included for purposes of explanation only, and it says not to attempt to use the information for actual implementations. It also notes that the algorithms and internal data structures are offered as suggestions rather than requirements, so implementers are free to design their own as long as the same external behaviour is achieved.
sections.plainLanguage: Domain names let a program ask for information about a name, such as the address of a host, without knowing where that information is kept. The request goes to a local resolver, which asks name servers on the network until it finds an answer. This RFC describes the pieces and the messages between them.

sections.title: Implementation Components
sections.content:
A host can take part in the domain name system in several ways, depending on whether it runs programs that retrieve information from the system, name servers that answer queries from other hosts, or both. The simplest configuration has a user program on the local host sending user queries to a resolver, which sends queries to a foreign name server and receives responses back, caching what it learns in a local database. User programs interact with the domain name space through resolvers, and the format of user queries and responses is specific to the host and its operating system; user queries will typically be operating system calls, and the resolver and its database will be part of the host operating system. Less capable hosts may implement the resolver as a subroutine linked into every program that needs its services. The resolver may have to make several queries to several different foreign name servers to answer a particular user query, so resolving one query may involve several network accesses and an arbitrary amount of time.

A name server can be a standalone program on a dedicated machine or a process or processes on a large timeshared host. The simplest name server acquires information about one or more zones by reading master files from its local file system and answers queries about those zones that arrive from foreign resolvers. A more sophisticated name server also acquires zones from foreign name servers, by periodically establishing a virtual circuit to a foreign name server to acquire a copy of a zone or to check that an existing copy has not changed; the messages sent for these maintenance activities follow the same form as queries and responses, but the message sequences are somewhat different.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver is the part of a host that answers questions about names. A name server is the part that holds the records and answers questions from other hosts. A host may be one, the other, or both.

sections.title: The Name Server Message Format
sections.content:
All messages sent by the domain system are divided into five sections, some of which may be empty. The header is always present and specifies which of the remaining sections are present and whether the message is a query, an inverse query, a completion query or a response. The question section contains a query type, a query class and a query domain name. The last three sections have the same format, a possibly empty list of concatenated resource records: the answer section holds records that answer the question, the authority section holds records that point toward an authoritative name server, and the additional records section holds records that relate to the query but are not strictly answers.

The header contains a 16-bit ID assigned by the program that generates the query and copied into all replies, a QR bit saying whether the message is a query or a response, a four-bit opcode, and four one-bit flags: AA, authoritative answer; TC, truncation; RD, recursion desired; and RA, recursion available. It ends with a four-bit response code and four 16-bit counts giving the number of entries in the question, answer, authority and additional sections. The opcode values are 0 for a standard query, 1 for an inverse query, 2 for a completion query allowing multiple answers, 2 for a completion query requesting a single answer, and 4 to 15 reserved for future use. The response code values are 0 for no error, 1 for a format error, 2 for server failure, 3 for a name error, 4 for not implemented and 5 for refused, with 6 to 15 reserved.

A resource record carries a name, a two-octet type that says what the data means, a two-octet class, a 16-bit TTL giving the time in seconds the record may be cached, a 16-bit RDLENGTH giving the length of the data in octets, and the data itself. A TTL of zero means the record can only be used for the transaction in progress and should not be cached, which is why SOA records are always distributed with a zero TTL.

Domain names are expressed as a sequence of labels, each a one-octet length field followed by that number of octets, and a name is terminated by a length byte of zero for the root label. The high-order two bits of the length field must be zero, which limits a label to 63 octets or less, and the total length of a domain name is restricted to 255 octets or less, so printed names are 254 octets or less. To save space, the octets that define a name may be terminated by a pointer to a previously specified label string; pointers are a two-octet field whose high-order two bits are ones and whose low-order 14 bits give an offset from the start of the message. Programs are free to avoid using pointers in datagrams they generate, though all programs are required to understand arriving messages that contain them.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain system message has a header, a question, and up to three lists of records. The header says which kind of message it is and how many records each list holds. A record says which name it is about, what kind of information it carries, and how long it may be cached. Names are written as labels with a length byte in front of each one, and a pointer can stand in for a name that has already been written earlier in the message.

sections.title: Resolver Algorithms
sections.content:
When a user requests a resource associated with a particular domain name, the resolver turns the user query into a number of shared database accesses and queries to remote name servers. It first checks the local shared database for the desired information; if it is found, the resolver checks the applicable timeout, and if that check succeeds the information is used to satisfy the user request. Otherwise it consults the shared database for the name server that most closely matches the domain name, where multiple redundant name servers may be found. It then chooses one of the available name servers and sends off a query; if the query fails it tries another, and if all fail an error indication is returned to the user. If a reply is received, the resolver adds the returned records to its database and interprets the reply. If the reply contains the desired information the resolver returns it to the user. If the reply indicates that the domain name does not exist, the resolver returns an error to the user. If the reply contains a transient name server failure, the resolver can either wait and retry the query or go back and try a different name server. If the reply does not contain the desired information but does contain a pointer to a closer name server, the resolver goes back to the step where the closer name servers are queried.

Several modifications to this algorithm are possible: a resolver may not support a local cache and instead cache only during the course of a single user request, discarding it on completion, and it may find that a datagram reply was truncated and open a virtual circuit so that the complete reply can be recovered. Inverse and completion queries have to be treated in an environment-sensitive manner, because the domain system does not provide a method for guaranteeing that it can locate the correct information.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver looks in its own cache first. If the answer is not there, it finds the name server that looks closest to the name being asked about, sends it a query, and either answers the user or follows the referral it gets back to another name server.

sections.title: Name Server Maintenance
sections.content:
Name servers perform maintenance operations on their databases so that the data they distribute is accurate and timely, and the amount of work depends on the size, change rate and complexity of the database. Maintenance operations differ for authoritative and non-authoritative data: a name server actively tries to keep authoritative data accurate by refreshing it from master copies, while non-authoritative data is merely purged when its time to live expires. The refreshing scheme is fairly simple but less powerful than those used in other distributed database systems: an update to the master does not immediately update copies, and should be viewed as gradually percolating through the distributed database. Where timeliness is critical, the master name server can prohibit caching of copies or assign short timeouts to copies.

Most information in the domain system is derived from master files scattered among hosts that implement name servers; some name servers have no master files, others have one or more. Each master file holds the master data for a single zone of authority rather than for the whole domain name space, and the administrator of a zone controls that zone by updating its master file. Other name servers become authoritative for a zone by transferring a copy of it from the server holding the master copy, using a virtual circuit; these copies include parameters specifying the conditions under which the data in the copy is authoritative, which in the most common case are a refresh interval and policies to follow when the refresh cannot be performed. A name server may acquire multiple zones from different name servers and master files, but it must maintain each zone separately from others and from non-authoritative data.
sections.plainLanguage: Each zone of names has one master copy on disk. Other name servers hold copies and refresh them from the master over the network. A change to the master therefore reaches the rest of the system gradually, as each copy is refreshed.

sections.title: Domain Support for Mail
sections.content:
Mail service is a particularly sensitive issue for users of the domain system, because there was no consistent system for naming mailboxes and even hosts, and because existing services had to keep working. Most mail systems specify a destination with a two-part construct such as X@Y, where X is often a user or account and Y is often a host; the memo calls X the local part and Y the global part. Most existing mail systems route mail on the global part alone, which the memo calls agent binding, where the mailer decides which host to contact using only Y. More sophisticated systems use both parts and separate the binding of the destination to the host from the actual delivery, which the memo calls mailbox binding; the global part can then be a generic name rather than a single host.

The domain support for mail has two levels. Agent binding is compatible with existing ARPA Internet mail procedures and maps a global part onto one or more hosts that will accept the mail, using the MAILA query type; it returns MD records specifying hosts expected to have the mailbox and MF records specifying hosts expected to forward the mail on. The hosts are hints rather than definite answers, since the query is made without the full mail destination specification. Mailbox binding offers extended services that map a local part and a global part onto one or more sets of data using the MAILB query type: hosts that will accept the mail, mailing list members, and mailboxes for reporting errors or requests to change a mail group. A query can return a name error, a Mail Rename record carrying a new mailbox specification, an MB record with the domain name of a host, one or more Mail Group records identifying members of a group, or an MB record together with Mail Group records.
sections.plainLanguage: The system can answer a mail question in two ways. The simpler one routes on the host part alone. The richer one looks at the whole address, so an organization can use its own name for a mailbox and hand out a list of people to receive mail at it.
